newsitem.title: HUNGARY: No NATO/Russia deal before enlargement-Kwasniewski.
newsitem.headline: No NATO/Russia deal before enlargement-Kwasniewski.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Tuesday it would be unrealistic to expect NATO to reach an agreement with Russia over enlargement before new applicant states are invited to join.
NATO is due to name its first new members for almost two decades at a special summit in Madrid next July at which it also hopes to crown a new deal with Russia.
"It is not necessary and I think this is unrealistic," he told Reuters in an interview. "I think until the Madrid summit we will have a lot of meetings, talks and discussions but no charter."
Kwasniewski was speaking at the end of a two-day working visit to Hungary at which Warsaw's and Budapest's aspirations to join NATO and the European Union were high on the agenda.

NATO hailed a five-hour meeting on Monday between alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov as positive, but said deep differences remained over alliance enlargement plans.
"I am sure this first meeting of Mr Solana (with Primakov) was the first round of a very long boxing match," Kwasniewski said.
"(But) it is a wrong approach to say that if the charter is necessary it is a necessary condition to enlarge NATO -- the enlargement of NATO and charter disucssions are parallel processes."

"There will be no treaty (in time for the Madrid summit) because Russia is not interested in speeding up this process of enlargement," he said. "Now Russia until the Madrid summit will do what is necessary to stop enlargement."
Kwasniewski added said he believed that once Russia sees that NATO will go ahead with eastward expansion without Moscow's agreement, it will seek a deal.
"If the enlargement goes on with no country slowing the process, Russia will be more and more flexible," he said
In a speech earlier to Hungary's Foreign Affairs Institute the Polish president appealed for a similar deal to "the NATO-Russia charter" for the Ukraine.
"The adaptation of the European structure will not be complete without satisfying the security requirements of Ukraine," he told his audience.
"As preparations to discuss the NATO-Russia Charter are being initiated, no effort should be spared to achieve a similar confirmation of the Alliance's partnership with Ukraine."
Ukraine, which borders Poland, once held more than 1,800 nuclear warheads but transferred the last of its share of the former Soviet nuclear arsenal to Russia for dismantling last year.
It has not asked for NATO membership but does participate in the alliance's Partnership for Peace friendship programme and hopes to win its own security guarantees from NATO.

In the same speech on Tuesday, Kwasniewski reiterated the year 2000 as a target date for Poland's accession to the European Union. EU officials have cast doubt on such a deadline, saying the complicated accession process could take at least two years longer.
French President Jacques Chirac said last week in Budapest, as he had done in Poland, that such a target date was achievable for Central European countries if there was the "political will".
Kwasniewski denied the target date was unrealistic.

"I am in a special position," Kwasmiewski told Reuters. "If President Chirac talks before the Polish parliament about 2000 for Polish membership of the EU, if (German) Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl is speaking about 2000, what can I as the President of Poland say?".
